In one case, then, we would have taken the pensioners' roll and lowered to 60 the age of eligibility for all the needy. Such an option, Mr. Speaker, can be ideal. It does not however take into account the fact that many Canadians are beginning to have doubts about retirement age; they want it to be optional and flexible. Canadians would rather not have a compulsory retirement age, namely 65. They would prefer to choose their own, a few years sooner or later, according to their personal circumstances.
I do hope we can find a way to distribute pensions because, to my mind, therein resides the whole practical problem of distributing pensions that leave room for the principle of flexibility and choice in one's retirement age. But we are not there yet. I shall be very anxious to get the recommendations of the Senate committee on the matter. But to say today that everyone of 60 to 65 who is in need should receive the federal pension automatically would cost the state $630 million more each year. In times of economic restrictions, that argument becomes important for the very simple reason that $1 billion already go each year to the provinces from all Canadian taxpayers, through the federal government, to pay for 50 per cent of the costs of all social welfare programs.
Needy people between 60 and 65 have to apply to their welfare office and withdraw the amounts for which they are

eligible. So the question becomes rather whether this should be paid for by the federal or by the provincial government.
We are now covering the spouses of pensioners who have already a right to their retirement and who are in need, which makes about 75,000 persons. Mr. Speaker, we have returned to the debate on the second reading of Bill C-5, which contains two proposed amendments to the Old Age Security Act. Sometimes I have the feeling that the very walls of this chamber must be so accustomed to speeches by me on the subject of pensions that those walls themselves should almost play my speeches back. But I hasten to assure not only the walls of this chamber but the members of this House that there are many more such speeches still to come.
If hon. members on the Liberal side imagine that they know what I am going to say about this bill, namely that it is good as far as it goes but that it does not go far enough, I assure them I will not disappoint them. That is precisely the position my party and I take respecting Bill C-5. The things which are in it are good and move in the right direction, but they do not go
Old Age Security Act
far enough. However, because the things in the bill move in the right direction, we shall be voting for it.
In view of the fact that the bill is set up in such a way that although the $20 increase in the guaranteed income supplement will not come into effect until January, 1979, but that the change with regard to the spouse's allowance will come into effect as soon as the bill has had royal assent, I feel the minister's request that we not delay the handling of this bill is one to which we ought to respond. It is my hope that the various stages through which the bill must go will not take very long.
Before I talk about the bill itself, the things in it which are good and the failure of the bill to go far enough, I confess I want to say a few words about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). I realize that opposition members, to be in character, must see no good in any member of the present cabinet. It is not very difficult to take that stance in respect of most of the members of the cabinet. But there are two or three-I do not think I would go much higher than that, though there may be four-who, in my view, have their priorities straightened out. One of those ministers is the present Minister of National Health and Welfare. I hope that is not the kiss of death; I would not want to do that to her!
If the rumours are correct that a cabinet shuffle is in prospect, I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will not move the present minister. I have noted with intense interest the speeches she has made. In fact, I have read, if not in full, certainly I have scanned them, all of the speeches she has been making all over the country, and it is clear that she is aware or has become aware of the shortcomings of some of our social programs. She is proud of the programs that have been put in place, and she has the right to be proud, but her awareness of the inequity of income distribution, her awareness of the high proportion of our people who are in the lower income brackets, and particularly her awareness of the difficult time that many of our older people are having, make her one whose voice in the cabinet is very important.
The spokesman for the official opposition who took part in this debate just before the vote we took at 5.45 referred to the fact that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is limited by the policies of the government in what she can do. It was a critical statement he made, but I think even that criticism carried with it the implication that if she could do better, she would.
1 compliment the minister on the speeches she has been making and on the efforts she has been putting forth to try to win some significant improvements in our social legislation. I have referred to her discovery about the large numbers of our people who are in the lower income brackets. She had something to say about that this afternoon.
I want also to refer to her discovery-and maybe this comes about because before she was in this department she had the portfolio of the minister of national revenue-that our income tax structure is one in which there is a host of hidden benefits

Old Age Security Act
for the wealthy. She has made a move to counter that by winning certain changes in respect of family allowance payments, and we will get to that when we get to another bill. Her proposal, even if it is in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), that there be income tax credits-and by "credits" we understand that to mean not just figures on a page somewhere, but actual dollars being paid out-granted to persons whose incomes are below certain levels is an indication of the awareness of the minister that there is an awful lot that is wrong with our income tax structure. It is, as I say, full of hidden benefits which exemplify the biblical statement that to them that hath is given. I commend her for having made a start in that direction.
I was interested in her reference this afternoon to the guaranteed annual income or to a negative income tax, or something like that. It was in character for her to blame the provinces for not having been willing to agree to it, but at least she is aware of that sort of thing.
I have no hesitation in commending the minister for the speeches she has been making and for the battling she must have had to do in cabinet to get some improvements in social legislation at this time. After all, the government tells us this is a time of restraint, and there are cuts being made, all over the place. If in such an atmosphere one minister is able to bring before the House an increase in certain social payments, it is obvious she did not accomplish that by suggesting it just once; she must have had to fight for it for a long time. 1 commend her for that, and if she can stand life in that cabinet much longer I hope she wins further gains.
I want also to commend the minister for taking the time this afternoon to dispel some of the myths about pensions and pension policies. I think she dispelled only two or three this afternoon, but she made at least one speech in which she lists seven of them and dispels them all. I am glad she took the time to point out that the campagin some people wage against pension indexing is completely without foundation. She was quite clear on that, and that just as other members of our society have the right to expect an increase in their incomes to keep up with the rising cost of living and, perchance, to keep up with a rising standard of living, that right should also be extended to pensioners.
I am glad that she took the time to point out that the arguments some people make that if we keep on doing so much for pensioners-and those words "so much" are not mine, but words other people have used-the day will come when everybody will be my age or older and there will not be anybody left to do the work. The minister gave statistics this afternoon to set that right. I have said many times in this House that perhaps the best legislation the Parliament of Canada has passed in my lifetime has been legislation in the social field. I am not going to give that fatherly or avuncular lecture I sometimes give about conditions as they were before I came to this House, but 1 will take a moment to say that 1 did have the good fortune of being alive and active in the 1930s, so I have a memory of what life was like for older people before there was

extensive government intervention to see that they got their rights.
I happened to be just 34 years of age when I came to this place back in 1942, and it was not very long after, largely because I succeeded the late J. S. Woodsworth who had something to do with the first old age pension legislation, that I became a spokesman for the older generation of that day. Now that my friends who were in their thirties when I came here are, along with me, members of the older generation, I am glad and honoured still to be one of their spokesmen.
So, Mr. Speaker, even though as a member of the opposition I am supposed to get up and condemn any minister for what was said at the beginning of a speech, I have to say that to me it was a delight to sit here this afternoon and hear the minister speak with pride about our pension legislation, to make it clear that it is here to stay, that things like indexing have to continue and that we have to continue to make other improvements for our older people.
There is no doubt that we have done a lot in the years since I first came here. In those years about all we were doing-and it took all of our efforts-was trying to get the amount of the opinion increased. When I came here the pension was only $20 a month payable at age 70 and then only with a means test. For years we worked hard on getting the amount increased, on getting the eligible age brought down and on winning universality. We have moved on from that to hospitalization and medicare, first for older people and now for everybody. We have moved on to housing for our senior citizens. I am particularly proud of the good job that was done in that field in my province during the years that Premier Schreyer was the leader of the government. We have established programs like, "New Horizons" and we have made all sorts of changes that have really been revolutionary.
I said that I was not going to repeat some of the things which I have said so many times here, but at this point I feel 1 have to say again that I well remember those days when our parents or our grandparents were at home in the back room, kept alive but that is all. They were not out in society They did not have clothes to wear or car fare. Car fare was something you spent on streetcars in those days, in case some members come from cities where they do not have streetcars.
Today many older people have their own apartments, and even if they are at bingo, at least they are out. I saw a sticker on a car the other day that I thought was very interesting. It said, "Support bingo, keep grandma off the street." I say that in the jest which the sticker intended, but I think that even in reciting it I can convey to hon. members-in fact, I am trying to impress upon them-that we have changed quite radically the life of our older generations. It just does not compare, the life of older citizens today, with what it was when I first became active in public affairs. To me this parliament has been worth it, to me our party has been worth it, if we have done nothing else. To me the years I have spent here have been worth while even if that was all we had achieved.

If I am taking a moment or two like this to speak with pride about what we have done, it is not just to be historical; it is because I am terribly concerned that there be no retreat from that position, that there be no rolling back. Every time I hear talk about privatizing or cutting government expenditure or the government getting out of the economy, I get afraid of what some of us knew and experienced when the government was not in the economy in the way it is today. I was delighted to listen to the speech which the hon. minister made this afternoon, and she has my support and backing as she continues to try to get social improvements out of the cabinet of which she is a member.
Having said that, sir, I should like now to get to the terms of the bill. I said at the start that members opposite knew before I began what I would say, namely, that the things that are in the bill are good but they do not go far enough. Certainly the $20 per month increase, whether it is $20 for a single pensioner or whether it is $20 for both partners of a married couple, is good. It still leaves many of our people on levels below the poverty line, but the $20 increase is good. I was delighted when I realized, soon after the announcement was made, that the minister won that as $20 across the board for those receiving the guaranteed income supplement, that it was not graded in some way. In other words, if a person is getting $50 or $60 guaranteed income supplement he still gets the $20; or if a person is getting only $1 guaranteed income supplement he still gets $20. Well, Mr. Speaker, let there be no doubt about it-and I am saying this on the opposition side of the House- that is good.
So, what is wrong with the bill if it is so good? Nothing is wrong with it, it is just what it does not do. The minister said this afternoon that 60 per cent of the people of my generation, a generation which is over 65, have little or nothing else. That is attested to by the fact that they qualify for guaranteed income supplement. I have been boasting about what parliament has done in the 40 or 50 years that I have been following these matters, but when 60 per cent of our older people have for their retirement only what they get from old age security and the guaranteed income supplement, this is a terrible condemnation of our economy, of our so-called private enterprise.
These are the people who have worked to build up this country and have made their contribution, and they now have to rely on so little, and they have to listen to speeches about the desirability of privatizing things and getting the government out of the economy. That being the case, that 60 per cent of our older citizens have so little else that they qualify for all or part of the guaranteed income supplement, I want to remind the minister that there is another bracket just above that where people are also in trouble. I am glad that she is by this legislation in effect raising the ceiling.
My arithmetic, which I hope is not far out, shows that when this plan is in full flight the 60 per cent will probably be 65 per cent, the 100,000 or so that were to be added. That 65 per cent of our older citizens have nothing else; they gain nothing because of the greatness of this private enterprise economy,
Old Age Security Act
but they are taken care of at the level of old age security and guaranteed income supplement provided for in the legislation of this parliament.
But just above that 65 per cent there will be another, I would guess, 20 per cent of older citizens who are in difficulty. The top 10 per cent or 15 per cent of those of us who are 65 years of age or older are all right. I am basing that statement on statistics that have been produced from time to time by the minister's own department. Quite frankly, I think 10 per cent is quite generous, but people between that 65 per cent level and the 90 per cent figure, another 25 per cent or 400,000 or
500,000	older Canadians-we are not talking just about a few, we are talking about 400,000 or 500,000-have just enough other income that they do not qualify for the guaranteed income supplement. There are certain benefits and perquisites that adhere to the guaranteed income supplement which these people do not get.
I wish, with the skill she has shown in getting money out of a cabinet that is cutting back and in getting something done about some of the unfairnesses in our income tax laws, she would give her attention to that group of people.
I know my simple solution has been rejected, that is, to raise the basic amount of old age security and adjust income tax so that the few at the top will have to pay most of it back. I make that proposal time and time again and I will go on making it, although it is difficult to win. In the meantime, there is that group of Canadian senior citizens, that group from 65 per cent to 90 per cent, which is about 25 per cent of the two million- that is, 400,000 or 500,000-who are having a rough time. They do not all write to me, but many do and they describe their difficulties. That is what is wrong with this bill; it does not meet the needs of those people.
The minister can say to me that she could not get that much money out of the cabinet and could not get a universal increase across the board. I enjoyed the way she told us this afternoon that what the government is doing can be done out of government revenues without any new tax. That is true. It is interesting, however, that every time over the years I have proposed pension increases the government has said to me: "Look at what it would cost; certain new taxes would have to be imposed." When the government decides on increases that amount to a few hundred million dollars, however, all of a sudden taxes do not have to be raised.
I hope the minister will find some way to persuade her cabinet colleagues that further things should be done. I know they cannot be done in Bill C-5. This parliament is not over yet, however, although it has not very many months left. I plead that she give thought to that group of 500,000 senior Canadians who are between those two points, 65 per cent and 90 per cent of the senior citizens of Canada.
I stand by and repeat the plea that I have been making in this place since the early 1940s-that pensions should be universal without a means test and that the amount should be a lot higher.

Old Age Security Act
The clock always seems to move faster when I am speaking than at any other time, Mr. Speaker, so I had better get on to the other aspect of this bill.
The bill also provides for a continuing for six months of the spouse's allowance in the case where a younger spouse has lost the pensioner or older spouse. There is no doubt it is a good thing that is being done. Every month between 200 and 250 persons in Canada, most of them women, have this experience. Every month in Canada 200 to 250 persons, mostly women, lose the older spouse and the spouse's allowance. Indeed, the pension, the whole works, is suddenly cut off. That is one of the reasons I am glad to see this part of the bill is not designed to come into effect in January, but instead as soon as the bill has had royal assent. Let us get it over to the other place and hope they will not treat this pension bill as they used to treat pension bill years ago.
That just solves the problem for some of the 200 to 250 persons, not all of them. It solves it for those aged 64'/2 until they reach 65, but what about the woman who becomes a widow at age 61 or 62? She gets another six months' pension and then has to go on welfare.
I think what is wrong with the minister's defence of this is that she puts the whole business of spouse's allowance in the context of its having been desirable for the government to solve the problem of two persons trying to live on one pension. She now says that in that context what she is doing is valid, that it does not destroy that, that it does not start giving pensions to widows or single persons. But I still feel and I felt at the time that the whole basis of the spouse's allowance that was passed in this House in June, 1975, and came into effect in October, 1975, was basically wrong when it established a marital test.
This House knows how opposed I am to a means test by whatever name it is called. But I would rather provide a pension between ages 60 and 65 on a means test or needs test basis, if you cannot make it universal or available to all those out of the labour market, which is the way I would do it. Surely the single person, the widowed person, the divorced person, is just as much in need and has as much right to be on a pension with honour and decency, rather than on welfare, as the woman who can say she got a man-this business of saying to a woman between the age of 60 and 65, "If you are single or alone you cannot get a pension; that pension with all its prestige and honour is only for you if you have got a man who is over age 65."
I cannot blame the minister; she was not in the department at that time. I think she was parliamentary secretary to some other ministry and although parliamentary secretaries have certain advantages they have the disadvantage of having to keep quiet about a lot of things. So I cannot blame her.
The minister said one thing this afternoon that I rather liked when she indicated that this was a step which is resolving one problem connected with the spouse's allowance. The problem of the spouse's allowance will not be solved until it is replaced in its entirety by a pension for persons between the age of 60 and 65 on some basis-some basis that does not have a marital test. That is completely wrong. My answer is a universal

pension available, if you will, to all persons between ages 60 and 65 who are out of the labour market-universally available, 1 do not mean universally paid, as it is, to those over 65. That is my answer. If that is too costly and the government is not prepared to do that, then, certainly between ages 60 and 65 the government should make it available to all persons who are in need.
Even the spouse's allowance, the key to which is the marital test, also has a means test with it. I know the spouse's allowance works both ways and the same deal applies to a young man with an older woman for a wife as vice versa, but in 80 per cent of the cases of marriage in this country, the husband is older, and in 90 per cent or perhaps 95 per cent of the cases where the spouse's allowance is applied for, there is a younger wife. I have had lots of complaints from widows who became widowed between ages 60 and 65, but I have never had a letter from a man saying; "My old woman died and I lost the spouse's allowance."

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to participate in the second reading debate on this bill to amend the Old Age Security Act. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I consider this legislation as important and even essential. I think that many have overlooked the significance of this measure and in my speech I would like to rouse deeper interest in this question which is of concern to us all.
This measure is important because to our senior citizens it is an indication of our constant concern about their needs and their welfare, even in a period of budget restrictions. We owe it to ourselves to be aware of the plight of those of our senior citizens who have problems and urgent needs. By increasing the guaranteed income supplement, we prove in a concrete way to our senior fellow Canadians that our commitment toward their welfare will stand.
We as members of the House have to deal with bills which sometimes need to be explained. This bill was remarkably explained this afternoon by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and I understand that members of the Opposition have also given other necessary explanations. This bill is important, Mr. Speaker, because as it was pointed out this evening for the first time it will enable many old age pensioners to rise above the threshold of poverty. Of course it is difficult to define poverty which can be quite subjective. Some consider themselves poor with incomes that others consider comfortable. In addition, strictly in terms of income the needs of people vary, depending on whether a person lives in a city, in a village or even in the country. We also have in Canada different levels of incomes and needs according to the areas of our country. This is why the definition of the threshold of poverty is more than arbitrary.
Nevertheless, there have been some measures established which are very useful. Statistics Canada has published such a measure of low income, beginning in 1973. This is based on the premise that families which spend more than 63 per cent of their income on basic necessities such as food, clothing and

October 26, 1978

shelter are considered to have low incomes. These levels vary by size of area of residence, with the lowest level corresponding to rural areas, and the level gradually increases with the size of area of residence.
Since Statistics Canada figures are always retrospective- the latest ones are for 1977-we have to make some assumptions about the growth rate of these poverty lines, but if we assume that the consumer price index for 1978 rises about 9 per cent over 1977 and that the low income level rises at the same rate, we find that a pensioned couple will for the first time be up to the Statistics Canada poverty line even if they have no income apart from their basic old age security and guaranteed income supplement or spouse's allowance. There are about 40,000 couples in this group. Those with incomes from other sources such as the Canada Pension Plan or private pensions will be better off than this.
Some people will suggest, of course, that $20 is not very much. They may not appreciate how tight the budget is for some senior citizens, and this extra amount may be the difference between not quite making it and having enough to get by. [Translation]
The increase will not be enough to enable pensioners living alone to rise above the poverty line but it will certainly contribute to improving their lot and they will go from 74 to 80 per cent according to the standards of Statistics Canada itself. Pensioners living alone are faced with a particularly difficult situation because unlike married couples or those who qualify they do not share the cost of rent, property taxes, heat and food. One interesting feature of this bill is that unattached pensioners covered by the guaranteed income supplement will receive the same $20 monthly increase as married pensioners.
Since this $20 increase will be most helpful to our senior citizens, I would like to comment briefly on provincial programs which will be affected by this measure. Mr. Speaker, some provinces pay additional benefits to G1S recipients. This extra amount-known as "gain" in my province-adds to their income so that they can at least meet their needs. Given the higher supplement proposed in Bill C-5, there is a possibility of conflict. Should a province not change its ceiling on income level, it would thus deprive many of its senior citizens of this increase. Some provinces sometimes reduce their own contribution to the guaranteed income supplement when there is an increase in the federal benefit. A few moments ago I was talking with the minister to know whether she had received from the provinces the assurance that they would leave that increase to those who really need it. She told me that she did receive that assurance from only two provinces, British Columbia and Ontario, and I congratulate them on that. I hope the other provinces will do the same.
As for housing, Mr. Speaker, the minister also confirmed a moment ago that she had not received from any province the assurance that they would not touch that increase in order perhaps to replenish their coffers or help fill their deficits in housing. And that I find regrettable. I would like the provinces
Old Age Security Act
to show as much generosity to try and understand that needy people do need that increase today because of the galloping inflation we now have in this country. Anyway I hope they will avoid the old practice, namely that you have to erode an increase when needy people do need it.

Another potential problem is presented by old age pensioners who reside in institutions. As I understand it, it is a common practice in most provinces to charge residents a proportion of their pension to cover room and board, leaving them with a portion for personal expenses which is called a comfort allowance. Concern has been expressed about these pensioners residing in institutions. I realize that this is a very complex issue. Practices vary from province to province and there are situations where comfort allowances become meaningless because of the physical or mental impairment of residents. However, I hope as far as possible this increase will be permitted to help augment the personal funds of pensioners in institutions.
I might mention also the situation of pensioners living in subsidized rental accommodation. I hope they will be allowed to benefit from this extra $20 a month and that there will not be a rise in their rents to take advantage of this benefit.
I have mentioned the importance of the G1S increase to pensioners. I think we should not ignore this importance as an economic stimulus. An extra $290 million a year will be in the hands of low income elderly Canadians who will be able to purchase more in the way of basic consumer goods. We know they will be spending this money and in helping them we shall be helping producers and retailers as well.
I turn now to the other amendment which is contained in this bill. Its cost to the taxpayer is not nearly as great but it is also a valuable improvement to the program, one which will provide relief for recipients of spouse's allowance who are faced with a particularly distressing situation.

Most hon. members know that the spouse's allowance paid the younger spouse of an old age security pensioner lapses upon the latter's death. That is a problem the government had foreseen and accepted when those allowances were first paid, because it is inherent in the nature of the program which itself is limited. I am happy that the minister found a way to improve the tragic situation which must faced by the recipient who, in addition to losing one he or she holds dear, suddenly also loses the financial assistance afforded by the allowance. [English]
The logic of the spouse's allowance is very straightforward. The families with which this benefit is concerned have a direct connection with old age security through the pensioner's spouse and it is reasonable that their immediate income needs should basically be met through this program. I do not agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he says it is a marital criterion. I repeat, it has a direct connection with the old age security program. It did not make much sense that a couple receiving the old age
518

October 26, 1978
Old Age Security Act
security pension might also have to seek provincial social assistance to meet basic income needs.
There are many others in the 60 to 65 bracket who are not eligible for this allowance, including widowed, separated and single persons, and married couples where neither spouse is old enough to qualify for old age security benefits. Also their needs are important, and the minister has expressed her concern on many occasions for such groups and for other Canadians in vulnerable circumstances. But as they do not have this direct and current connection with the old age security program, it seems reasonable that their needs should be met through other programs.
This is a very important point to understand about the spouse's allowance. I have heard a number of criticisms of this program, but almost all of them are criticisms of other programs, most particularly the present system of provincial social assistance. Really they are stating that other programs are not as adequate, effective or attractive as the spouse's allowance and the old age security program in general.
Undoubtedly the good example set by programs like old age security and the spouse's allowance shows that efforts toward general improvements in the over-all Canadian system of social security must continue. But it upsets me to see good programs being criticized essentially because they are better than other parts of the current system.
Because the spouse's allowance is a limited program, however, it has been necessary to terminate the benefit if the younger spouse's connection to the old age security program is terminated, whether it be by separation or divorce, or by the death of the pensioner. We could not in fairness continue this benefit indefinitely when there are no further ties to the old age security program. It would not be fair to do so when so many others in the 60 to 64 age group in similar situations who would also like to benefit from the Old Age Security Act must be told that they are not yet eligible.
On the other hand, the wrenching, emotional experience of widowhood and financial loss is something that we all must sympathize with. The six-month extension proposed by the minister will help those caught in this situation, without going against the essential principle underlying the entire program. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I know many hon. members would like us to do even more than what is provided in this bill; I share their concern and wish to help their compatriots. But we cannot use the old age security program to solve all old age security problems in all social areas in Canada. Those problems can only be solved by improving other sectors of social security; I am confident that they can and will be solved. I shall mention only the initiatives already taken, through the changes made in family allowances and the income tax act we shall probably be looking into within the next few days, to help families generally through increases, changes in structure, changes in the programs and in the income tax act.


I would be guilty of exaggeration if I stated that the old age security program is perfect; it does not pretend to be. But it has been adapted to meet many of the changing needs of Canadian society. Let us look at the changes made to the program over the last 15 years. In 1965 the old age security program provided a flat rate benefit of $75 per month for Canadians aged 70 or over. Today, whether retired from the active work force or not, a Canadian aged 65 who meets the residence requirements will receive a basic old age security benefit of up to $164.74 a month. This is an indexed benefit which is revised quarterly to reflect rises in the cost of living and to maintain its purchasing power.
As well, the pensioner with little or no additional income can qualify for a guaranteed income supplement, which now amounts to as much as $102.61 per month for a married individual and $115.55 for a single pensioner. Soon this will be more. The spouse's allowance is also income tested and currently provides for the payment of up to $267.35 each month to the younger spouse aged 60 to 64 of an old age security pensioner. A retired couple in Canada can now receive monthly benefits of as much as $534.70 from the old age security program alone, and with the increase proposed, this amount will be more than $20 higher in January of 1979.
[ Translation]
The cost of improving benefits is not negligeable. But the importance of the program in meeting the needs of our old people is, I am sure, understood by all. That is why we shall continue seeking to further improve our old age security program, for instance, through the higher income supplements and broader spouse allowances as contained in this bill, without ever forgetting exactly where old age security fits in the context of our over-all Canadian social security system, through which we must continue to meet the needs of all Canadians.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES- LENGTHENING OF SEAWAY SEASON
TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES- LENGTHENING OF SEAWAY SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago in this House I had the opportunity in the middle of the strike on the seaway to ask about the efforts being made to keep the seaway open a good deal longer, given the backlog of grain and the need to move more grain to maintain a balanced economy and our balance of payments.
The strike on the seaway was extremely serious and there is no question that it was dealt with in that fashion. It lasted just about a week and then we had legislation overwhelmingly adopted to end the strike and put the ships back in operation. The fact that the House moved so fast, the fact that the economy of the country was in serious jeopardy because of this strike, highlights the extreme importance to the economy of Canada of the St. Lawrence Seaway and, of course, of the port of Thunder Bay.
Thunder Bay is the third largest port in Canada. In terms of grain tonnage we ship two-thirds of all the grain moved from the west out of Thunder Bay. Therefore, anything that closes down the seaway and the operation of the port of Thunder Bay is of vital consequence to the country, and certainly the speed at which we moved to terminate the strike illustrates that factor.
In the last six years many of my colleagues and I have fought hard to improve the St. Lawrence Seaway and to improve the facilities on it, as well as to lengthen its season. We fought to keep the tolls down, even though an agreement between the United States and Canada was in the offing which would have seen the doubling of the tolls over a one-year

October 26, 1978
Adjournment Debate
period. However, we gained the point that the tolls will be doubled over a three-year period, 50 per cent in the first year and 25 per cent in the subsequent two years. This is very important. I hope that the minister keeps in mind that the excess revenue which comes from this increase in tolls over this three-year period will be used to improve facilities on the seaway. Specifically, Mr. Speaker, to lengthen the season of traffic on the seaway.
Early this summer the ministry announced that a study had been initiated by the department using a firm of consultants to test the economic feasibility of lengthening the season ultimately to 11 months. This is extremely important, and certainly it would have been this year, with a slowdown because of the strike as well as a backlog of grain in the west, if everything had been in position to lengthen the season. But of course, this is not the case.
I understand the report is completed and the draft is in the hands of the ministry. I hope it will be tabled in this House within a month. I am sure it will indicate that there are great cost advantages to lengthening the period in which the seaway is open. We hope the minister will move as rapidly as possible, considering the extra revenue that is now being received.
If we can put class 10 icebreakers in the Arctic to move natural gas, oil and so on through a 12-month season, there is no reason why we cannot extend the life of the St.Lawrence Seaway to ten, 11 or even 12 months. It is important that we put pressure on the department in this direction. We hope that the result of this initial study will be out very shortly and that we will then move into some very progressive measures to keep the seaway open.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES- LENGTHENING OF SEAWAY SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) who for many years has been trying every time he gets a chance to do so to exert as much pressure as he can on the Department of Transport and people in general who have to make decisions concerning the St. Lawrence Seaway to improve that system that is truly vital to the economy of this country.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind him that since the St. Lawrence Seaway was opened in 1959 the seaway authority has been trying to find a way of extending the shipping season on that waterway. That research which is being carried out at a time when demand is much lower than the capacity of the system is motivated by the simple desire to make the system of locks and canals more effective.
The seaway, as anyone knows in Canada, met with much greater success than had been anticipated initially. So, last year, record volumes of 63.3 million tons of commodities were shipped between Montreal and Lake Ontario, and a record volume of 71.1 million tons was also moved that same year through the Welland canal. So it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the best way of increasing the capacity of the seaway and its

effectiveness is to extend the shipping season and, hence, the period during which the facilities can be used.
Already, without pomp or ceremony, Mr. Speaker, the season has been extended by a month from IVi to 8Vi months. The season now goes from April 1 to about December 15, and even last year the last ship to leave the seaway or the system did so on December 26.
So the seaway authority is developing an ongoing program to slowly extend the season, adding four weeks. That program will be gradually phased in on the basis of demand and also, of course, the advantages Canada will be able to get out of it.
The cost of this development is naturally increasing as the Seaway attempts to work under adverse cold weather conditions. Studies indicate just enough benefits to warrant this modest and gradual approach. We can therefore look forward to steady work and the long term goal of a season lasting 11 months, one month being used for annual lock maintenance.
A crash program to extend quickly the season because of unusual circumstances would likely be impractical. Much of the experience gained so far by the two U.S. and Canada Seaway entities and by the coastguards, indicates that more than positive thinking is now needed to achieve the objective. Sustained efforts and large amounts of money are required from now on to extend the navigation season further.
This effort must necessarily be a long term undertaking. I wish to stress that the interest of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) and the type of pressure he is constantly bringing to bear will certainly assist in having the season extended.

Mr. Speaker, on October 13 I posed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in relation to the sale or proposed sale of government inland terminals. I specifically asked whether the decision to sell the elevators was his decision or that of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and, second, whether the government would guarantee job security and security of pensions to those employed in the elevator system.
I received no response to the first question. I can only assume that the decision was not that of the Minister of Agriculture but rather that of the President of the Treasury Board. I believe the Minister of Agriculture has more sympathy than that for the farmer and is concerned about the sale of grain in western Canada.
Since 1972 I have pressed for the utilization of these inland terminals. The answer from the Minister of Agriculture, the minister in charge of the wheat board and the officials of the wheat board has always been the same, namely that they blame the line company elevators. They say the line company
October 26, 1978

elevators did not and do not want the terminals to be utilized to the fullest extent.
These terminals were built in the era of 1914 to 1920 approximately. They are all in pretty good shape at the present time. There are five terminals having a capacity of some 17 million bushels. They can supply half the needs of Vancouver harbour with grain prepared to export condition. I might point out that in Moose Jaw the elevator is operating 24 hours a day.
In the past these elevators have operated at about 20 per cent capacity yet they made a profit. I put a question on the order paper in 1976 asking for a statement of the profit and loss position of these elevators. I found that in the period from 1959-60 to 1975-76 the five terminals made a profit of over $4 million; if you add the profit of the Prince Rupert terminal the amount is brought up by more than S5 million. Yet the President of the Treasury Board in his statement announcing the sale of these elevators indicated that the sale was being carried out for the purpose of saving some $6.3 million. It is interesting to note that Mr. Mantz, the general manager of the terminal elevators, said he could not understand where the President of the Treasury Board got those figures because the elevators would this year show a profit of between $4 million and $5 million.
As I say, the Moose Jaw elevator has been operating since May 1 on the basis of three shifts a day around the clock. They are handling rape, flax, buckwheat and mustard and most of this is coming from the Alberta Pool, the Manitoba Pool and the UGG. All these companies are utilizing the facilities to the fullest extent. They evidently see a need for them and I suggest that the statements by the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the wheat board to the effect that the pools and the UGG do not wish to utilize these elevators are not correct.
It is unbelievable that the government should be wanting to sell these elevators when they have been operating at a profit. This year the profit will probably be larger in one year than the profits for the last ten years. The Hall commission recommended the utilization of the government elevators but the minister and the Canadian Wheat Board rejected the report. My opinion is that neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the minister in charge of the wheat board has ever sat down to discuss the proper utilization of these facilities. Certainly, in my opinion, they have never discussed the matter with the line companies or with the railways. The farmer-owned elevator companies are concerned about the maximum movement of grain on behalf of their members.
Our transportation and grain handling system is in a mess. Deliveries this crop year are 33 per cent down compared with last year. Surely the time has come to make a realistic attempt to develop and improve that system. I believe these inland terminals must be part of our grain handling arrangements.
I understand these terminals are worth $120 million. What will they be sold for? I do not think a buyer will be found at that price. My personal feeling is that they should not be sold.
Adjournment Debate
At most they should be leased. They should be operated at cost. If there is a sale there should be a condition attached that the elevators must be utilized to the maximum, otherwise the sale would be void and the facilities would be returned to the taxpayers and used by the government.
I am concerned also about job security for the employees. If a sale takes place it should be a condition that the job security of these permanent employees as well as their pension rights will be protected.

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to respond to the hon. member's question. The Canadian government elevators consist of five inland terminal elevators at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Calgary, Edmonton and Lethbridge, and one terminal elevator at Prince Rupert. The total licensed capacity of the six elevators is 541,870 tonnes. The total licensed capacity by elevator is as follows: Moose Jaw, 154,020 tonnes; Saskatoon, 154,020 tonnes; Calgary, 70,010 tonnes; Edmonton, 65,510 tonnes; and Lethbridge, 35,000.
The amount of grain handled by the inland grain elevators in 1977-78 was as follows: Moose Jaw, 21,163 tonnes; Saskatoon, 140,709 tonnes; Calgary, 55,778 tonnes; Edmonton, 57,413 tonnes; and Lethbridge, 22,000 tonnes. Current projections for the 1978-79 crop year are that the amount of grain handled at each of the inland grain elevators will be higher in 1978-79 than in 1977-78.
The current projection for operating profit for the 1978-79 crop year is that it will be higher than in any of the six previous crop years. This will be as a result of the substantial increase in revenue coming from the increase in grain handling. The net operating profit-before depreciation-in the last six years was as follows: 1972-73, $1,051,375; 1973-74, $765,458; 1974-75, $2,056,081; 1975-76, $2,531,461; 1976-77, $838,377; and 1977-78, $1,301,180.
The five inland grain elevators were all built between 1914 and 1931 with the Moose Jaw and Saskatoon elevators being built in 1914, the Calgary elevator in 1915, the Edmonton elevator in 1924, the Prince Rupert elevator in 1926 and the Lethbridge elevator in 1931. All of the elevators have been maintained in good working condition, considering their age, through a regular program of structural repair and maintenance. The five inland grain elevators are each equipped to dry grain and to clear grain to meet export standards.
The Canadian government elevators have not been utilized to their potential physical capacity. The government has announced that the elevators are to be sold to the private sector. We are optimistic that this initiative will enable these elevators to be used more in line with their potential.
The Department of Agriculture is now drawing up the conditions for the sale of the inland grain elevators. We feel that the elevators must be operated in the interest of the grain farmers of western Canada to assist in realizing market opportunities for Canadian grain.

October 26, 1978

FINANCE-TAX RECOMMENDATIONS OF ECONOMIC COUNCIL OF CANADA

Mr. Speaker, the question I put to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) yesterday concerned the fifteenth annual report of the Economic Council of Canada. I put to the minister the fact that the Economic Council has recommended this year, as it had last year, that the economy required, at the very least, the following three measures: cuts in income tax, cuts in the federal sales tax, and a federal-provincial capital works program to offset the difficulties that currently last in the construction industry, particularly in our metropolitan areas.
In his answer, the Minister of Finance simply indicated that he would take into account the recommendations of the Economic Council and that he was appreciative of efforts from this side as well as from other quarters to draw his attention to certain recommendations before the budget was brought down.
I think his answer raises two further problems, and they are the ones to which I should like to address myself this evening. The first is the fact that the economic priorities and economic direction of the government have been, it seems to me, severely criticized in the report of the Economic Council. Obviously the council will not put it that way, but that seems to be the implication of their report.
The second problem which is raised by the minister's answer is the totally unsatisfactory way in which budgets are prepared and in which economic advice is given and taken. We in the New Democratic Party have been arguing for many years that it was not good enough to have an Economic Council which would simply make recommendations to the government which could be ignored at any given time. The composition of the Economic Council of Canada depends entirely on the whim of the government. We in the NDP have argued for a form of social and economic planning which would allow a serious canvassing of opinion from all quarters of our society, not only those people who have the power to make representations.
If the Minister of Finance was asked who made representations to him concerning the budget, both formally and informally, I am sure the reply would not include many of the people who do not have power in our society. It is these two problems I wish to deal with this evening, briefly as it may be.
The first problem is that the government, by adopting the Tory policies of cutbacks, has assumed that these policies will somehow administer a boost to our economy, on their own and that they will be sufficient to stimulate an economy with a serious problem of industrial undercapacity and unemployment that causes tremendous human problems of which I am sure all hon. members are aware. The fact is that the cuts brought in by the government were brought in without any consultation, even with the cabinet of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and without any warning or systematic planning.
There have been a series of ad hoc emergency measures to deal with a set of long term problems, and they are simply inadequate. One cannot cut $2.4 billion off a budget in the

space of two weeks or one month without creating havoc within the government or great hardship and unfairness toward individuals.
In particular, I should like to direct the government's attention to the fact that the immediate implication over a period of a year or two of cutting back the amount of benefit paid in unemployment insurance is to reduce considerably the level of demand in our economy. It will take money out of the economy which would otherwise be there. If I am not mistaken, the estimate of the Minister of Finance indicated that demand would be reduced by $1 billion. While that type of cut might seem attractive to the bankers of this world, certainly it will do nothing to stimulate consumer demand or protect the living standards of ordinary Canadians.
Yesterday in my speech I had occasion to recite the figures from Statistics Canada concerning the fact that more and more families were forced below the poverty line as a result of the anti-inflation measures of 1976 and 1977. I guarantee the number will be increased as a result of measures introduced by the government since August 1978.
Coupled with these cutbacks is the assumption that the private sectors will fill in the gap. It is that myth which the Economic Council attacks directly. It has pointed out that, in order for that to take place, it would require an increase in consumer spending and private investment which has been unheard of in the country for the past 50 years. That will not happen.
The second point I wish to emphasize is that it is no longer possible to continue consulting with different power groups in this ad hoc manner. That does not amount to economic planning and consultation. The government should look at the proposals of the New Democratic Party respecting economic planning, particularly the mechanisms which allow us to consult fairly with all groups, and propose a budget over a period of time which allows the House, and the many groups outside it, to be consulted about the economy of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its Fifteenth Review, the Economic Council of Canada has once again made a useful contribution to the discussion of Canadian economic problems and the policies necessary to deal with them. Of course, this is not to say that I agree with all their policy proposals.
I should like to begin my discussion of the council's recommendation for a $2 billion cut in personal income tax or manufacturers' sales tax by noting that there is much more to the council's discussion of fiscal policy than the specifics of its recommendation. Indeed, the council wrestles with many of the same issues that the minister must face in preparing the budget. It should come as no surprise that the council emphasizes that the policy choices he must make at that time are, indeed, difficult.
On the one hand, expansionary initiatives such as the tax cut could improve the short-term outlook for real growth and

employment. On the other hand, there are also concerns over the exchange rate and inflation. The minister is now in the process of preparing a budget. He will have to form judgment about the relative magnitudes of these various effects of expansionary initiatives and how to weigh them off one against the other. He has some difficult choices to make. He is concerned about employment, but at the same time he is determined to bring down the rate of inflation. To find out what his choices are we will have to wait until budget night.
The council observed that the cumulative increase in public debt relative to national income or to the tax base has raised questions about the government's room for manoeuvring. To shed some light on this issue, the council presents figures on the general government deficit as a percentage of gross national product for Canada and for the other major OECD countries. These figures show that the Canadian general government deficit at all levels, both federal and provincial, while at 3 per cent of GNP, is, indeed, greater than in the United States, but smaller than in other countries such as West Germany, Japan and Italy.
The council interprets the international comparison of government deficits as suggesting there is perhaps room for
Adjournment Debate
additional fiscal stimulus. This is not to say it does not regard the deficit as worrisome. Others may interpret the figures differently. The minister will inform us of his interpretation on budget night.
The Economic Council has come forward with its review at a good time. Its tax cut recommendation and supporting analysis must be welcomed as a useful input to the budget making process. It will be given full consideration, just as are all the other pre-budget submissions the minister receives.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to commend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae) who, in less than 30 hours as a member of this House, has raised two questions, made his initial speech and been on the late show. I would defer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I think that must be some kind of record.
